intents.answer: Here is how Aqil usually answers: "At MSI I managed the data system for USAID third-party monitoring across 10 active projects. Monthly processing used to take about 20 analyst hours. I rebuilt it as a Python pipeline from Survey123 to Power BI with automated validation and row-level security, and it dropped to about 8 hours, around 60 percent less. More importantly, red and yellow flags reached mission leadership faster, so problems at sites were followed up sooner."

Here is how Aqil usually answers: "At Adroit we were collecting tens of thousands of interviews for several UN evaluations at once, and errors caught late would have meant costly re-visits. I set up automated R validation that ran on incoming data every day and flagged duplicates, outliers, GPS and skip-logic problems back to the field supervisors while teams were still in the area. That validation covered more than 40,000 interviews. The lesson I took: build quality checks into the process, not at the end."
follow: How does he ensure data quality?

intents.answer: Here is how Aqil usually answers: "I treat data quality as a process from the start. First, good tools: forms with skip logic, constraints and GPS. Second, well-trained enumerators who understand every question. Third, daily automated checks in Python or R for duplicates, outliers, timing and logic errors, with a QA log fed back to supervisors. Fourth, back-checks and spot checks. Finally, I document every cleaning rule, so the numbers in the dashboard can always be traced back to the raw data."

Here is how Aqil usually answers: "I start from the decision the person needs to make, not from the data. I lead with the answer in one or two sentences, show one clear visual, and keep the technical detail ready if they ask. For USAID mission leadership, that meant a dashboard with simple red and yellow flags instead of tables. I also check understanding by asking what they will do with the finding."

When there is a disagreement, for example on a method or a deadline, I listen first, bring the data or the options with their trade-offs, and agree on a way forward with the person who owns the decision. Then I support that decision fully."

Here is how Aqil usually answers: "I have led field and data teams on large evaluations and monitoring programs, for example managing the collection of more than 40,000 interviews at Adroit with the field and data teams, and coordinating monitoring of 12 programs at ACE. I lead by setting clear standards, training people well, and giving quick, kind feedback. I have trained more than 500 staff and partners, and I want my next role to include leading and mentoring a team."

Here is how Aqil usually answers: "Third-party monitoring runs on monthly and weekly deadlines, often for several projects at once, so I plan backwards from each report date and agree priorities with my manager early. I automate repeat work, which is why I built the Python pipeline at MSI, and I flag risks as soon as I see them instead of at the deadline."

Here is how Aqil usually answers: "My role at MSI ended in March 2025. Since then I have done focused consulting work in evaluation and data, completed my MBA, and earned my Oracle SQL certification. Now that I am settled in Maryland, I want a long-term role with a U.S. organization where I can grow into leading a data team."

Here is how Aqil usually answers: "In five years I see myself leading a data or MEL team: building reliable data systems, mentoring analysts, and helping leadership use evidence in their decisions. I want to keep growing technically too, especially in data engineering and AI tools, while moving toward director-level responsibility."

Here is how Aqil usually answers: "I like that good data changes real decisions. In my field work I saw programs adjust because a monitoring report showed what was not working, and I want to be the person who makes that evidence reliable and easy to use."

Here is how Aqil usually answers: "I follow informed consent and do-no-harm in every data collection, train enumerators on confidentiality, and keep personal data out of analysis files and reports. Access is controlled, for example with row-level security in Power BI, and I never share client data outside the project. That is also why every dashboard on my portfolio uses simulated data."

Here is how Aqil usually answers: "I worked fully remotely for MSI from 2022 to 2025 with teams in different locations. I keep remote work smooth with clear written updates, shared trackers, and short regular check-ins, and I make my dashboards the single source of truth so everyone sees the same numbers."

Aqil usually asks things like: "What decisions will this role's data support in the first six months?", "How does the team handle data quality today, and where does it break?" and "What would success look like for this role after one year?"

Modeled on the endline evaluation of a girls' science education pilot in 13 government schools, where I was the Data Analyst (TAGHEER, 2021): I trained the data collection team on the tools, then cleaned and analyzed the quantitative and qualitative data from 473 students, parents, teachers and officials and prepared the analysis datasets for the report.

Paired t-test on baseline and endline marks for the same students. Club vs non-club: Welch t-test on gains with Cohen's d, then an OLS model with grade and school fixed effects and robust standard errors, so the club effect is not just a school effect. Attitudes: top-2-box on five-point Likert items. The analysis is written in Python and again as a Stata do-file.

Modeled on the quantitative final evaluation I worked on, under the team's lead researcher, as Quantitative Data Analysis Consultant for Premium Performance Consulting (2024 to 2025): a BMZ-funded livelihoods and resilience program in six provinces covering cash-for-work, unconditional cash transfers, livestock support, kitchen gardens and solar-powered water systems for more than 21,500 vulnerable households. I built the indicator framework, sampling and tools, and ran the disaggregated analysis.

Food Consumption Score (FCS): weighted days of eight food groups over 7 days, grouped Poor / Borderline / Acceptable using the WFP thresholds. Reduced Coping Strategies Index (rCSI): five weighted coping behaviours; 19+ is treated as high coping. MDD-W: share of women 15 to 49 eating at least 5 of 10 food groups. Tests: Welch t-test and chi-square for baseline vs endline, and a logistic regression of acceptable FCS on sex of household head, province, intervention and household size. The R script and Python results match row for row.

Item analysis: percent correct (difficulty) and item-rest correlation (discrimination) for every test item. Reliability: KR-20 for the full 12-item test. Modeled on an ILO-funded assessment by Adroit Associates (2022) of occupational safety and health good practices in small and medium businesses in Balkh that had been trained under the Road to Decent Jobs for All Afghans project. The real assessment used semi-structured interviews and checklist-based observation with before and after comparisons (passageway marking, lighting and ventilation, fire safety, first aid, supervision).

Each business is observed twice, so every checklist item is a paired yes/no outcome. McNemar's exact test per item shows which changes are larger than chance. A business-level compliance score shows whether gains are broad or driven by a few businesses.
